Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

papers.title: Structure and Binding of the \texorpdfstring{$pnΩ^-$}{pnOmega} System with a Near-Unitary \texorpdfstring{$NΩ$}{NOmega} Interaction from Physical-Point Lattice QCD
papers.summary: The binding and spatial structure of the \(pnΩ^-\) system are investigated in the \(I(J^P)=0(5/2^+)\) channel using the physical-point HAL QCD \(NΩ({}^{5}S_2)\) interaction. The pairwise Hamiltonian includes the spin-triplet \(pn\) interaction and the finite-size Coulomb attraction in the \(pΩ^-\) pair. The three-body Schrödinger equation is solved with the Gaussian Expansion Method (GEM), including all three Jacobi rearrangement configurations. For the central HAL QCD potential at \(t/a=14\), the calculated three-body binding energy is \(18.63\) MeV, corresponding to a separation energy of \(16.39\) MeV relative to the \(d+Ω^-\) threshold. The spatial structure is examined through interparticle root-mean-square distances, pair and spectator radial distributions, and the correlation between the two Jacobi coordinates. Relative to a frozen-deuteron folded reference, the full three-body solution exhibits a substantially more compact spectator distribution and a contracted \(pn\) pair. The dependence on the Euclidean-time choice of the HAL QCD potential is also assessed. The results characterize the three-body rearrangement induced by the attractive \(NΩ\) interaction within the adopted pairwise model.

papers.title: AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications
papers.summary: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.

papers.title: Adaptive Tests of Pricing Restrictions with Observed and Latent Factors
papers.summary: This paper develops a high-dimensional test for asset pricing models with observed and latent factors. The null hypothesis allows the intercepts from an observed-factor regression to be nonzero, provided that they lie in the latent factor loading space. We estimate the pricing errors in three steps: regress returns on the observed factors, extract latent factors from the lagged covariance structure of the regression residuals, and regress returns on both observed and estimated latent factors. The intercept from the final regression serves as the estimated pricing error. We construct Sum and Max tests based on the estimated pricing errors to detect diffuse and concentrated alternatives, respectively, and combine them using a Cauchy procedure. Under suitable regularity conditions, we establish the joint null distribution of the component statistics, their asymptotic independence, and their power against alternative hypotheses. We also propose a residual bootstrap and establish its first-order validity. Simulation studies examine the finite-sample performance of the tests under different pricing-error patterns and factor-number choices. An application to S\&P 500 stocks illustrates the use of the proposed framework in evaluating an observed-factor pricing model after latent-factor adjustment.

papers.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
papers.summary: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

papers.title: Ab-initio cryo-EM reconstruction from moments of denoised images
papers.summary: In single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), high-resolution three-dimensional (3-D) refinement requires a reliable ab-initio model to converge to the correct structure. Both refinement and existing ab-initio methods estimate the orientations of the particle images together with the 3-D structure, which can be slow for large and noisy datasets. We present a method of moments approach that bypasses orientation estimation and recovers a 3-D ab-initio model from the first three moments of denoised images. On experimental datasets, our method produces ab-initio models rapidly and successfully initializes high-resolution refinement. This is the first successful application of method-of-moments-based ab-initio modeling to experimental datasets without assuming a uniform distribution of orientations.

papers.title: Thermodynamic topology and orbital dynamics of charged RN--AdS black hole with logarithmic corrections
papers.summary: This study investigates the topological thermodynamic properties and orbital dynamics of the Reissner--Nordström anti-de Sitter (RN--AdS) black hole with logarithmic corrections solution in Einstein--Maxwell gravity. By utilizing the Duan's $Φ$-mapping theory, we investigate the topological classes within the generalized three-parameter Sharma--Mittal entropy formalism. Employing different thermodynamic ensembles, including the canonical and mixed canonical ensembles, we explore the critical, divergence points and heat capacity, which help us determine the thermodynamic stability of the BH. In addition, the Hamiltonian formalism is employed to investigate the orbital and oscillatory motion of neutral test particles. By utilizing the effective potential approach, we examine the effective force, the stability of circular orbits, and the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). We further analyze the trajectories of test particles and derive the radial $\left(ω_{r}\right)$, latitudinal $\left(ω_θ\right)$, and azimuthal $\left(ω_φ\right)$ oscillation frequencies, together with the periastron precession frequency. This work provides key insights into the fundamental nature of Einstein--Maxwell gravity. Moreover, these results provide a comprehensive theoretical description of the orbital dynamics of the RN--AdS black hole solution and may be useful for future high-precision astrophysical observations.

papers.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
papers.summary: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.
papers.comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 14 tables, including supplementary material

papers.title: Dynamical Variational Theory of Stochastic Reaction Networks
papers.summary: Discrete stochastic population dynamics describe systems ranging from biochemical reaction networks and gene regulation to epidemic spreading, ecology, and population genetics, where finite populations generate strong intrinsic fluctuations. Predicting their dynamics, including mean populations, fluctuations, time-lagged correlations, response functions, and steady states, remains challenging: the chemical master equation admits no general analytical solution, numerical solutions scale poorly with system size, and standard approximations fail at low copy numbers. Using a field-theoretic representation of the reaction dynamics, we develop a dynamical variational approximation for stochastic reaction networks based on the Plefka expansion from spin-glass physics. For reaction systems with general stoichiometry and time-dependent rates, the expansion yields tractable non-Markovian effective dynamics with self-consistent memory. We further introduce a generalized self-consistent bubble resummation that provides closed predictions for means, correlations, and response functions. The formulation applies broadly to discrete stochastic population dynamics on networks, and we provide a numerical implementation with adaptive time stepping for user-defined systems. We benchmark the method on stochastic gene regulation, enzyme kinetics, and infection dynamics, where it accurately captures both time-dependent behaviour and steady states, including fluctuation-driven effects missed by conventional approximations. Together, these results establish a general analytical framework for stochastic reaction dynamics across transient and stationary regimes in strongly fluctuating low-copy-number systems.

papers.title: Measurements of inclusive $J/ψ$ production in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 14.6, 17.3, 19.6, and 27 GeV with the STAR experiment
papers.summary: Inclusive $J/ψ$ production at mid-rapidity ($|y| < 1.0$) in Au+Au collisions at center-of-mass energies per nucleon-nucleon pair ($\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$) of 14.6, 17.3, 19.6, and 27 GeV is measured with the STAR detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. The nuclear modification factor $R_{\rm AA}$ is used to quantify modifications of $J/ψ$ production relative to an interpolated $p$+$p$ reference. The measured $R_{\rm AA}$ shows a hint of a decreasing trend from peripheral to central collisions, reaching a value of approximately 0.5 in the 0-20% centrality class across all collision energies. Unlike similar measurements in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 200 GeV, where $J/ψ$ $R_{\rm AA}$ shows little dependence on transverse momentum ($p_{\rm {T}}$), the corresponding $R_{\rm AA}$ at the lower collision energies of 14.6-27 GeV shows a tendency to increase with $p_{\rm {T}}$. Additionally, the inclusive $J/ψ$ $R_{\rm AA}$, integrated over $J/ψ$ $p_{\rm {T}}$, in central collisions exhibits no significant variation within uncertainties over the energy range of 14.6 to 200 GeV. These results can be qualitatively described by transport models that incorporate hot and cold nuclear matter effects.

papers.title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference
papers.summary: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.

papers.title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform
papers.summary: This paper presents HAVAPlot, a browser-based framework for scientific visualization and post-processing of numerical simulation data. Operating entirely within the user's browser, HAVAPlot requires no software installation or data uploads while supporting mesh-based and tabular datasets beyond computational fluid dynamics. The framework directly reads native OpenFOAM cases, including polyhedral meshes, ASCII and binary fields, boundary data, and Lagrangian particles, as well as legacy and XML VTK files and tabular datasets. It provides line, contour, and three-dimensional plots; exact polyhedral slicing; boundary extraction; variable calculations; customizable color scales; symmetry mirroring; zoomed insets; streamlines; isosurfaces; particle visualization; and vector PDF/EPS and data export. The underlying numerical algorithms are independently verified. Cell centers and volumes agree with an independent implementation of OpenFOAM's geometric algorithm, while 6.1 million field values across four two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional production cases are reproduced to machine precision. For analytical fields on distorted hexahedral meshes, cell-to-point interpolation exhibits second-order convergence in the interior and first-order convergence at boundaries. Meshes containing 250,000 cells load in at most 1.3 seconds. Applications to an impinging supersonic jet, hypersonic cylinder flow, a hybrid particle-continuum cold-spray nozzle, a three-dimensional gas-bearing film, and supersonic cone flow demonstrate the framework's capabilities.

papers.title: Fractional Order or False Memory: Identifiability of Caputo SIR Models from Incidence Data
papers.summary: When a fractional order improves the fit of an epidemic model, it is usually taken as evidence of memory. We ask whether the order of the Caputo susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model can actually be recovered from incidence data. If the transmission rate is allowed to vary freely in time, as in hybrid forecasting models, every admissible order, removal rate and initial count reproduces the data exactly. With constant transmission and exact data the order is identifiable in principle, but the dominant term of early linearized growth depends on only two parameter combinations: the growth rate r = (beta - gamma)^(1/alpha) and the amplitude beta*I0/alpha. What is left is transient, and it is limited. We prove that parameter sets sharing these two combinations give Poisson count distributions whose Kullback-Leibler divergence stays bounded no matter how long the linear phase is observed, and that the nonlinear model inherits this bound as the population grows. In simulations, wrong orders were rejected in at most 5% of replicates when the data ended two weeks or more before the epidemic peak, and in 95-100% once the peak was included; separation began only a few days before the peak. With mild overdispersion the order was identified only once about 60% of the population had been infected, and with stronger overdispersion not even then. Fits that the early data could not tell apart predicted peaks that differed by 75%, and plug-in forecasts that ignored parameter uncertainty were badly overconfident. Data generated without any memory produced fitted orders below one when transmission changed and when the fitted model was discretized in daily steps. In early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States, orders from 0.6 to 1 gave almost the same growth rate, whatever value we assumed for the removal rate.
papers.comment: 25 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24357533

papers.title: GenAI-DBT: Evaluating a DBT-Informed Generative AI Platform for Mindfulness Skills Training: A Pilot Randomized Study
papers.summary: We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and engagement of three digital formats for dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) mindfulness skills training. In a 30-day randomized pilot study, 45 university students were assigned to GenAI-DBT, a general-purpose large language model chatbot (Chatbot), or a static web resource (Web). Forty-two completed the study, and nine completed follow-up interviews. Usability scores were within acceptable ranges across conditions, with no significant between-group differences. GenAI-DBT showed the highest observed participant-week adherence (71.4%, vs. 53.3% for Web and 42.3% for Chatbot), a descriptive difference. Mindful Attention Awareness Scale and Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale scores showed no significant time-by-group interactions, and session-level self-reported mood changes did not differ significantly across conditions. GenAI-DBT showed a larger positive change in linguistic valence than Chatbot (4.28 vs. 1.59, P = .02, Cohen's d = 0.99). Interviewees valued contextualized, scenario-based practice and identified response latency, repetition, and limited personalization as areas for improvement. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of DBT-informed conversational AI for skills practice and motivate further evaluation in larger, more clinically relevant samples. Clinical efficacy remains to be established.
papers.comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Jingchen Ye, Yujia Chen, and Leyang Han contributed equally. Yucheng Jin is the corresponding author

papers.title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
papers.summary: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

papers.title: Structural Fine-Tuning under Economic Restrictions
papers.summary: How should a predictor trained on historical data be adapted to a new economic environment or task when few target observations are available? We propose structural fine-tuning, a framework that introduces economic restrictions to guide the adaptation of pretrained predictors. The framework does not require a complete structural model; instead, it utilizes constraints based on economic knowledge, ranging from simple, ubiquitous assumptions to particular workhorse models. Theoretically, we characterize conditions when economic restrictions improve prediction over the original model and ordinary fine-tuning. Then, we illustrate the framework through a simulation exercise of a credit issuer's credit-limit decision following a Medicaid-style expansion in medical payments. Imposing restrictions based on eligibility, outstanding medical bills, cash flows, and group-level risk bounds, our framework lowers the root mean squared error of predicted risk by 28 to 39 percent and the issuer's policy regret by 3 to 10 percent relative to ordinary neuron gating, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Single-fit inference for the realized prediction error of a logistic model with many predictors
papers.summary: When independent validation data are unavailable, evaluating a fitted logistic model on new patients requires estimating prediction error and uncertainty. Evaluating the fit on training data is often optimistic. Bootstrap validation is widely used to correct this bias, but with many predictors, it can retain bias and yield unreliable confidence intervals. In this article, we study these limitations and develop single-fit estimation and inference without resampling. When the number of Gaussian predictors grows proportionally with sample size, we analyze unpenalized logistic models. We prove that standard bootstrap correction can have nonzero limiting bias even as the resample count grows and location-shifted intervals can have zero limiting coverage. Instead, we adjust the fitted scores to consistently estimate realized Brier and log losses. We account for common fitting and adjustment error to construct valid marginal intervals and joint regions. We also establish these single-fit estimation and inference guarantees for certain non-Gaussian designs in proportional dimensions. Under moderate dimension growth and possible misspecification with general predictors, we extend single-fit inference to ridge regularization and construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals for realized log loss. Simulations and analyses of hospital and diabetes datasets support our theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
papers.comment: 77 pages, 2 figures. Replication code and numerical results are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24356958

papers.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

papers.title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization
papers.summary: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.

papers.title: Cognitive Constraints and Misspecification Concern
papers.summary: We study repeated decision problems in which an agent has cognitive constraints and is concerned that her models might be misspecified. She first uses data to weight candidate models, subject to a cognitive-capacity constraint on the complexity she can process, and then she evaluates choices according to how well they perform under those models. More data need not overcome limited capacity: a statistically inferior but simpler model can remain relevant in the long run. When the constraint binds, evidence that favors models in proportion to their complexity can leave current behavior unchanged while still affecting later responses to data. This constraint eliminates cycles between risky and safe actions when simple models favor safety, and relaxing it can make risky play more attractive initially yet less frequent in the long run. It can also sustain misspecified model classes by suppressing choices that would reveal their errors.

papers.title: Quantum Calibration of Local-Volatility Surfaces from Sparse Option Quotes
papers.summary: Calibrating a volatility surface from sparse option prices requires repeated solutions of a pricing equation as the volatility parameters change. We implement a hybrid quantum and classical method for this inverse problem using the Dupire local-volatility model. A positive coefficient representation specifies the local variance, and linear combinations of Hamiltonian simulations approximate the associated pricing evolution. The circuit propagates through successive maturity intervals and evaluates discrepancies at the observed strikes. Measurement counts provide the objective values used by a classical optimiser to update the volatility coefficients. We implement this calibration cycle in a logical gate simulator and assess it alongside classical pricing solvers and alternative surface models. Multiple-maturity synthetic examples illustrate the reconstruction of smiles and skews, while a separate small circuit experiment tests the complete measured calibration. The comparisons quantify the effects of model flexibility, pricing approximation and measurement precision. Recorded gate counts and sampling budgets identify the main computational costs of the implementation.
papers.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027), IEEE Symposium on Computational Intelligence for Financial Engineering and Economics (IEEE CIFEr). Code: https://github.com/khoshisashi/quantum-local-vol

papers.title: Networked wealth and mortality in the Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System, 2009--2018
papers.summary: Background. Though resources embedded in social networks appear to shape health, past studies have not assessed this relationship directly. Using data from Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System in South Africa, we examined the spillover effect of household wealth on mortality in the family network. Methods. We analysed cohort data from 2009 to 2018 to estimate the Average Total Effect (ATE) of household wealth on deaths, decomposing this into an Average Direct Effect (ADE) and Average Spillover Effect (ASE). We estimated these quantities separately for all deaths, deaths among children (<5 years old), premature deaths (among ages 15-59), and deaths among elders (60+). Results. Over the study period, 8750 individuals died. Overall, a one standard deviation increase in household wealth led to an ATE of -0.61% (95% CI: -0.74 to -0.48, P<0.001), an ADE of -0.53% (95% CI: -0.63 to -0.42, P<0.001) and an ASE of -0.08% (95% CI: -0.18 to 0.01, P=0.075). For premature mortality, these effect estimates were -0.37% (95% CI: -0.47 to -0.26, P<0.001), -0.29% (95% CI: -0.37 to -0.21, P<0.001), and -0.08% (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.00, P=0.038), respectively. Conclusions. Results provide evidence for the protective effect of household wealth on premature mortality across family relationships.
papers.comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 1 box, supplementary appendices S1-S4. Accepted for publication in the American Journal of Epidemiology (manuscript AJE-00063-2023) in 2023 following peer review; final manuscript submitted January 2025; not yet published

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
papers.summary: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
papers.comment: 16 pages, 7 tables, 5 figures, 1 appendix. Companion paper: arXiv:2607.22397. Code: pip install nimbus-bci (v0.9.0)

papers.title: Modeling Learner-Technology Interaction Through Multilevel Gaze Transition Dynamics to Inform Usability in Online Learning
papers.summary: Gaze data provide fine-grained evidence of how learners engage with instructional content and interface elements, complementing conventional usability evaluation methods. However, eye-tracking analyses often examine within-slide visual attention and across-slide navigation separately, limiting understanding of learner interaction throughout extended learning experiences. This exploratory multi-method study integrated area-of-interest transitions, gaze entropy, slide-level navigation, and network-based representations to analyze seven eye-tracking recordings of high school students interacting with an AI-supported online biology lesson, complemented by three post-intervention focus groups. Results showed individual differences in within-slide gaze allocation and switching patterns. Learners followed shared navigation pathways but differed in revisiting and immediate return behaviors. The focus group findings highlighted positive perceptions of interactive materials and AI-generated feedback, alongside usability concerns related to navigation, interface clarity, and assessment guidance. Together, these outcomes show how integrating multilevel gaze analytics with learner perspectives can provide complementary evidence for identifying interaction trends relevant to usability evaluation. Future research should test this approach with larger, more diverse samples and examine relationships among gaze patterns, usability, and learning outcomes.

papers.title: Folk Theorems for Social Learning
papers.summary: We study repeated games with purely informational externalities. Each player observes a single conditionally independent signal and then repeatedly takes publicly observed actions to maximize their expected discounted payoff, which depends only on the state and their own action. We show that, when there are sufficiently many players and they are sufficiently patient, there exist equilibria where information is aggregated: the players' payoffs approximate the full-information payoff. This holds even if actions are uninformative under myopic play. Conversely, even if myopic play reveals the state, there also exist equilibria where information is not aggregated: payoffs approximate those under autarky. Our results speak to the range of possible outcomes of social learning games with forward-looking agents.

papers.title: AI-Induced Social Erosion: Using LLMs for Work Tasks Reduces Help-Seeking Intentions Towards Colleagues
papers.summary: Generative AI is becoming embedded in knowledge work as an intelligent collaborator to assist in completing tasks. However, this readily available assistance risks displacing key interactions through which colleague relationships are built and sustained at work. This paper leverages the concept of help-seeking behaviour to investigate whether and how AI usage shapes colleague relationships. We conducted an online experimental vignette study where 248 knowledge workers evaluated scenarios that systematically varied whether and how AI was used across different work tasks. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that AI-enabled work reduced help-seeking intentions compared to non-AI work across tasks, and especially for brainstorming. Visible AI usage was associated with greater help-seeking intentions towards colleagues, and individual contributors' colleague relationships were more vulnerable than managers. Our findings identify opportunities for workplace AI tools, practices, and policies to preserve colleague relationships in increasingly AI-integrated workplaces.

papers.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
papers.summary: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of a Body-Machine Interface as an Alternative Control Paradigm for Pedal-based Sewing Machines
papers.summary: Body-machine interfaces (BoMIs) exploit body movements to control assistive devices; they have been evaluated primarily in tasks such as cursor control or robotic manipulation where the entire movement repertoire is devoted toward device control. However, tasks with multiple concurrent processes require the user to share the movement repertoire used for device control with other body movements for task execution. This issue is examined here in the context of sewing, where the sewing machine is typically controlled by a pedal in coordination with hand movements for guiding the fabric. We evaluated the learning of a trunk-controlled BoMI for sewing machine control, and compared it with conventional pedal control. Twenty-four novice participants (12 BoMI, 12 Pedal) completed 10 trials of a standardized sewing assessment followed by 3 trials of a transfer task. The BoMI mapped trunk movements to the sewing machine's full functional repertoire, which included continuous speed control of the needle, and discrete actions such as presser-foot and needle lifts. The two groups learned at comparable rates, showing similar completion times and error counts; for both groups, completion time reduced by approximately 30\%. Additional analyses showed that the BoMI group had fewer presser-foot lift errors during training and fewer errors on the first transfer trial. Both groups also exhibited similar subjective workload. These findings collectively demonstrate that a BoMI interface can support sewing-machine control during concurrent manual activity, highlighting the potential for using BoMIs for increasing accessibility in industrial workplace contexts.

papers.title: Towards Restorative Urban Spaces: An Exploratory Field Study of Nature Videos on Public Multi-Display Signage
papers.summary: In recent years, multi-display signage (MDS) has become increasingly common in urban stations, plazas, and other public spaces, where it is primarily used to present advertisements and information. Beyond these conventional applications, MDS offers opportunities to shape people's experiences of public environments through spatially distributed and dynamic visual content. Motivated by the potential of mediated nature to support restorative experiences in urban environments, we conducted a nine-day exploratory field study in a free-admission area of a science museum, presenting artificial intelligence (AI)-generated nature videos across four displays and collecting 1,263 questionnaire responses. We combined three complementary analyses. First, structural equation modeling identified strong associations among perceived consistency across displays, presence, and self-reported restorative responses, consistent with our theoretically motivated model. Second, exploratory comparisons across video-presentation configurations revealed modest differences in consistency and restoration ratings, although these AI-generated videos did not significantly outperform the advertisement reference. Third, qualitative analysis of open-ended responses identified fascination, immersion, and restorative feelings, alongside concerns about naturalness, visual quality, and motion-related discomfort. Together, these findings provide empirical insights into MDS-mediated nature experiences, with implications for nature-video design and questionnaire refinement. They also inform a tentative conceptual extension of the model incorporating additional perceptual and evaluative factors.

papers.title: Informative Local Average Treatment Effects Using Propensity Scores
papers.summary: In instrumental variable (IV) models, comparisons of conditional local average treatment effects across covariates can mix effect heterogeneity in observed covariates with changes in the complier population, that is, those whose treatment responds to the instrument. Compliers at different covariate values may differ in unobserved characteristics that may also drive effect heterogeneity. We propose informative conditional local average treatment effects (ICLATEs), which condition on a subset of covariates of interest and on the treatment propensity scores under both values of a binary instrument. Fixing these scores holds constant the range of unobservables that drive treatment selection and thus compliance, while the composition of the covariates not conditioned on may change. Under conditional IV assumptions and suitable support conditions, we establish nonparametric identification and characterize the relationship of the ICLATEs to marginal treatment effects. We distinguish effect homogeneity in the unobservables driving treatment selection from effect homogeneity across excluded covariates. We clarify their roles in extrapolating complier effects to population effects and show that, jointly, they yield a testable implication even with a single binary instrument. For estimation, we combine cross-fitted machine learning of the nuisance functions with pooled local linear regression of doubly robust scores. Under undersmoothing and regularity conditions, we establish pointwise asymptotic normality, which a simulation study supports. As an empirical illustration, we apply the method to the Job Corps program to assess how the earnings effects of training participation vary with age.

papers.title: Stability Bands for Feature Attribution: The Core, the Nucleolus and the Bargaining Set of Explained-Variance Games
papers.summary: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends $2β_iβ_jσ_{ij}$, so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.
papers.comment: Presented at the XXV Jornadas Latinoamericanas de Teoría Económica (JOLATE 2026), San Luis, Argentina, October 29, 2026. 24 pages, 5 figures

papers.title: Network-Adaptive Instrumental Variables
papers.summary: Three mechanisms generate endogeneity in regressions under interference. We address them by constructing network-adaptive instrumental variables (NIV) for a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model with endogenous covariates and unknown network weights. Under network-conditional exclusion and information equivalence, the resulting instruments yield valid moments without knowing the true network. We establish joint identification of the structural mean coefficients and the network parameters, providing two sufficient routes. Then under additional covariance restrictions, we identify the disturbance spillover coefficient and the innovation variance. We develop NIV-GMM estimation, establish consistency and asymptotic normality, and give feasible inference and a test for mean network spillovers. Monte Carlo simulations examine their finite-sample performance.

papers.title: Crisis Governance at the Joints. Mapping the Ethical and Societal Territory of Crisis Management Technologies: The Case of Human-Swarm Teaming
papers.summary: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

papers.title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
papers.summary: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.

papers.title: Cultural invariance in music-evoked emotions
papers.summary: Worldwide, people produce and listen to music to induce, express, and regulate their own and others' emotions. To what extent culture influences the emotions evoked by music is, however, contested. The documented global variation in musical behaviours and emotion concepts suggests substantial cross-cultural differences in how listeners relate to music emotionally, while shared physiology and evolutionary history would predict broad global agreement on the emotional information extracted from music. Some evidence suggests shared processes but experiments on the subject do not represent global diversity in either music or participants. Here, we report a large citizen-science experiment wherein listeners (N = 124,394 in 189 countries; conducted in English) rated their emotional responses to popular Western music and to vocal music produced in mostly small-scale societies drawn from a globally representative corpus (i.e., songs assumed to be unfamiliar in style). We found strong similarity in listeners' emotional responses to music: Average agreement between pairs of countries' listeners was high. Furthermore, across both popular and unfamiliar types of music, emotional responses were shaped far more by individual listeners and the specific songs than by cultural background: Both between-person differences within a country and within-subject differences across songs explained substantially more variance in emotional responses than country-wise differences. Together, these results indicate that a listener's cultural background has only a marginal influence on the emotions they feel in response to music, raising the possibility of universal structure in emotional responses to music.
papers.comment: Data, code, materials, and supplementary information are available at https://github.com/themusiclab/music-emotions

papers.title: Open Response Explorer: a Structured Collaborative Writing System for Peer-Informed Open-Response Assignments
papers.summary: Peer-informed open-response assignments (where students view, connect, and learn from peer contributions) hold the potential to foster collaborative knowledge building, yet the unstructured nature of free-form prose prevents students from effectively comparing and making sense of peers' work. We present Open Response Explorer, an interface that recenters open responses on structured idea units through purpose-based writing and peer response exploration, augmented by common-role text segment highlighting for easy comparison. A within-subjects lab study (N=12) validated the usefulness and usability of the system, demonstrating how it shaped the open-response drafting and peer exploration practices. We discuss implications for purpose-centered authoring and exploration that transform free-form prose into structured, comparable, and collectively navigable knowledge artifacts.

papers.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Survival Regression with Time-Varying Covariates and Random Effects
papers.summary: In longitudinal survival studies, biomarkers and treatments change across visits, their associations with event risk may be nonlinear and change over time, and subjects with identical measurements may differ in risk. Existing tree-ensemble survival models address these features separately: discrete-time formulations accommodate covariate updates without subject-specific random effects, and hazard-based ensembles with frailty take covariates as fixed at baseline. We propose Time-Varying Survival Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (TVSurvBART), a continuous-time hazard model combining a flexible baseline, a log-linear tree ensemble, and subject-specific random intercepts and slopes; covariates enter as predictable step processes, and interval-start time among the tree inputs lets effects change across visits. Integrated exposure offsets absorb the within-interval variation of the baseline and random slopes, so the tree leaves retain conjugate updates. Re-centering moves along likelihood-invariant directions and alternating centered and non-centered covariance updates address the resulting posterior dependence. In two simulation families, TVSurvBART's landmark predictions from held-out subjects' histories up to the landmark time have higher time-dependent AUC than the Cox, frailty Cox, and forest benchmarks in every setting and lower Brier scores in all but one comparison, although population-summary gains are not uniform. In the CARRA juvenile idiopathic arthritis registry, discrimination for recorded flares is similar to Cox regression, while a secondary interval-probability score favors TVSurvBART.

papers.title: Persistence of Multifractal Dynamics at the Mammalian Neuromuscular Junction Across Extracellular Calcium Conditions
papers.summary: The neuromuscular junction represents a relevant experimental model for revealing important biophysical mechanisms underlying synaptic transmission. In this work, we revisited the time-series analysis of electrophysiological recordings obtained from mammalian diaphragm neuromuscular junctions. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA) to assess whether intervals between spontaneous potentials exhibit multifractal behavior at physiological extracellular calcium concentrations and at hypocalcemic and hypercalcemic levels. Surprisingly, we observed a robust, stable multifractal profile across all electrophysiological recordings, regardless of calcium concentration. Therefore, our results provide support for a rich and complex scenario governing neurotransmitter release. Based on these findings, we discuss their biophysical significance and physiological implications.

papers.title: The Scaled Dirichlet Distribution: Lauricella Representations and Estimation
papers.summary: We derive explicit expressions for the mixed moments of the scaled Dirichlet distribution in terms of the Lauricella hypergeometric function of type $D$. The relationship with Carlson's multivariate $R$-function is stated, and the convergence conditions required for the series derivation are made explicit. The general expressions yield means, second moments and covariances, with Gauss and Appell hypergeometric representations in the bivariate and trivariate cases. Method-of-moments and maximum-likelihood formulations are presented, together with simulation summaries and an illustrative comparison of scaled Dirichlet and ordinary Dirichlet fits to compositional futures-return data.

papers.title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
papers.summary: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.
papers.comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. R package discoCVI available on CRAN

papers.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
papers.summary: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

papers.title: A Human-Centric Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Digital Twin Framework for Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.summary: Digital twins of cyber-physical systems must operate with scarce data, on assets that change after deployment, and for humans whose needs differ, yet existing implementations fix fidelity at design time and do not match the representation to the human or the task. This paper proposes a human-centric adaptive multi-fidelity digital twin framework that models the evolving human, the physical twin, and the digital twin core, and adds a human inference and adaptation function that estimates the human state, predicts the response, and adapts the representation. The framework defines low-, medium-, and high-fidelity tiers distinguished by adaptivity and by coupling, quantified as the ratio of the digital twin latency to the duration of the process step it follows. Three proof-of-concept instantiations are evaluated: a virtual reality tutor, a computer numerical control milling model, and an industrial training station. The low tier estimated learner sentiment with an accuracy of 0.86. The forecasters of the milling model and the training station, both medium-tier, showed a normalized error decline of 0.39 to 0.89 and a human adaptation gain of 1.16 to 1.51, but their latency exceeded the physical process step by 25 to 87 times. Only the station's vision model met the physical step. The tiers are separated by which functions adapt and where the latency constraint lies, not by a monotone increase in gain or coupling.
papers.comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables; submitted to Advanced Engineering Informatics

papers.title: ShEPhERD-score: Fast, adaptable three-dimensional alignment of molecular features
papers.summary: Three-dimensional (3D) molecular similarity scoring and alignment are widely employed in ligand-based virtual screening and molecular design, and are increasingly used for training and evaluating machine learning models. Existing open-source methods utilize various molecular representations spanning shape, electrostatics, pharmacophores, and hybrid representations, but their implementations as independent software packages with distinct application programming interfaces (APIs), optimizers, and limited GPU support make them difficult to compare, combine, or extend. Here, we develop ShEPhERD-score into a unified, modular platform for differentiable 3D molecular similarity scoring and alignment by combining diverse molecular representations with high-performance Numba CPU and Triton GPU kernels to support both large-scale library screening and pairwise similarity workflows. In matched comparisons with open-source 3D similarity tools on the DUDE-Z virtual screening benchmark, ShEPhERD-score performed comparably or better in eight of nine cases. Across the scoring modes in ShEPhERD-score, throughput ranges from 17,800 to 1.03 million alignments/second for ten-million-conformer libraries using a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Moreover, we found that the most effective scoring mode varied by protein target, indicating that target-specific calibration against validation data may be valuable before large-scale screening and underscoring the need for a unified platform that provides diverse molecular representations. Together, these capabilities establish ShEPhERD-score as a single, extensible toolkit for rapid virtual screening and machine learning workflows.

papers.title: Naturalness scale inference in chiral perturbation theory and chiral logarithms
papers.summary: We infer naturalness scales of chiral perturbation theory in the mesonic sector using Bayesian techniques that are extended to explicitly take into account chiral logarithms. To demonstrate our approach, we consider the chiral expansion of the pion decay constant $F_π$ and the threshold and subthreshold parameters of $ππ$ scattering. We find a strong observable dependence of the inferred naturalness scales, and show that they need not coincide with the pion mass at which the order-by-order hierarchy of the chiral expansion breaks down. As an application, we discuss the requirements for lattice-QCD constraints on the two combinations of $O(p^6)$ low-energy constants that in the current matching of Roy-equation analyses to chiral perturbation theory need to be estimated from resonance saturation, but could be extracted from the pion-mass dependence of $ππ$ scattering parameters.

papers.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
papers.summary: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.
papers.comment: Accepted at the Thirteenth Annual Conference on Advances in Cognitive Systems (ACS), Edinburgh, United Kingdom, October 6-9, 2026. Awarded one of 2026 Ada Lovelace Awardees for Excellent Paper Submissions to ACS

papers.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

papers.title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
papers.summary: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

papers.title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
papers.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Intelligent Information Systems (Springer Nature)

papers.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

papers.title: Three-nucleon potentials and their matrix elements for $δ_{\mathrm{NS}}$ in superallowed $β$ decays
papers.summary: We derive three-nucleon potentials for radiative corrections at order $\mathcal{O}(αε_χ^2)$ in chiral effective field theory where $α$ is the electromagnetic coupling and $ε_χ$ is the chiral expansion parameter. These corrections contribute to the nuclear-structure-dependent term $δ_\mathrm{NS}$ for determinations of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix element $V_{ud}$ from superallowed nuclear $β$ decays. We compute matrix elements of three-nucleon contributions at orders $\mathcal{O}(α^2)$ and $\mathcal{O}(αε_χ^2)$ using quantum Monte Carlo methods. We find the matrix elements at order $\mathcal{O}(α^2)$ to be large and to have an effect on the extraction of $V_{ud}$ at the scale of $10^{-4}$. In the case of $^{10}$C, the matrix elements of $\mathcal{O}(αε_χ^2)$ three-nucleon operators provide a 2% correction to $δ_{\text{NS}}$, and are thus beyond the current precision goals. The relative size of three-nucleon corrections to $δ_{\text{NS}}$ in medium mass nuclei, where two-body contributions tend to be smaller, remains to be investigated. We then use these results to determine $V_{ud}$ from the superallowed transition ${}^{10}\mathrm{C}\rightarrow{}^{10}\mathrm{B}$.

papers.title: One size does not fit all: session-specific effects of deep brain stimulation on hand-motor kinematics in Parkinson's disease
papers.summary: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) effectively treats motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is unclear whether it changes fine hand movements in the same way for every patient. We analyzed 35 sessions of 19 patients with PD from a multi-center cohort performing the CopyDraw task, a drawing task designed to overcome the subjectivity and limited granularity of clinical assessments. Besides standard kinematics (mean velocity, acceleration, jerk, and drawing accuracy), we derived higher distributional moments and non-linear complexity measures, for 38 features in total. DBS effects were quantified with linear mixed models at the group level and with residualized regression and a random-effects meta-analysis per session. The DBS state was decoded per session with regularized linear discriminant analysis to compare feature sets as behavioral labels for deriving physiomarkers for adaptive DBS (aDBS). DBS modulated all 38 features at the group level, most strongly velocity-related features. However, for every feature, the between-subject variability of the DBS effect exceeded the group-level effect. Only one feature, the detrended fluctuation analysis of the distance to the template, showed a significant mean effect across sessions, and it is not a standard kinematic feature. In six sessions without any significant modulation of standard features, complexity measures were modulated instead. For decoding, standard features alone were the best choice in ten of 35 sessions, but combining all 38 features yielded the highest average area under the ROC curve (0.700 vs. 0.677), with the largest gains in sessions that were hard to decode from standard features. DBS effects on hand-motor behavior are individual. Deriving neural markers for aDBS from behavior therefore requires session-specific analyses with individualized features beyond standard kinematics and group-level effects.

papers.title: Data-driven simulation of the brain's response to stimulation: a system identification approach for closed-loop neuromodulation, piloted in adaptive deep brain stimulation
papers.summary: Closed-loop neuromodulation uses a physiomarker to control stimulation. Developing such controllers requires exploring a large space of strategies and parameters, which is often not feasible with the human-in-the-loop. Simulation environments offer an alternative. Adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS) for Parkinson's disease is a stereotypical application: while physiomarker identification progresses rapidly, clinically available control is limited to threshold and proportional strategies. We propose to identify dynamical models of the brain with and without deep brain stimulation (DBS) using the sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) framework. Identified ex post from existing recordings, such models are a middle ground between abstract bottom-up models and the realistic but difficult-to-access human-in-the-loop. Forecasting neural activity from real initial conditions, the models create a simulation environment for "what if" analyses of DBS changes. In a proof-of-concept with EEG data from a single subject, we train and evaluate threshold, proportional, proportional-integral-derivative (PID), and proximal policy optimization (PPO) control, aiming to have the simulated data classified as DBS ON at minimal energy. SINDy models fitted on spatially filtered EEG maintained DBS condition-specific characteristics. All aDBS controllers delivered DBS more efficiently than continuous DBS (cDBS), with up to 20.2% energy reduction. Proportional control yielded a small but significant gain over threshold control. PID and PPO achieved a comparable reward advantage over cDBS, with PPO stimulating more conservatively and PID saving the most energy. The approach thus proved feasible, and within this simulation environment, PID control is a strong a-priori choice, while the benefit of deep reinforcement learning may only emerge with richer physiomarker signals.

papers.title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
papers.summary: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort.
